description: This case study is the US National Transportation Safety Board report on the rupture of Enbridge Line 6B, a 30-inch crude oil pipeline, at Marshall, Michigan, on 25 July 2010, report number NTSB/PAR-12/01, adopted on 10 July 2012 (164 pages). The abstract states that the rupture occurred during the last stages of a planned shutdown and went undetected for over 17 hours, that twice restarting the line added 81 percent of the estimated 843,444 gallons released, and that oil saturated wetlands and reached the Kalamazoo River; residents self-evacuated and about 320 reported symptoms. The board finds corrosion fatigue cracks under disbonded tape coating and deficient integrity management, control centre and emergency response practices, and directs recommendations to the Department of Transportation, PHMSA, Enbridge, the American Petroleum Institute and others. Access: free PDF from the NTSB website; no licence is stated. Coverage is one pipeline incident and US regulation. Caveats: only the abstract and front matter were read here. It suits emergency response and hazard exposure studies of oil pipelines and leak detection, and no directly related records are catalogued yet.

name: Enbridge Incorporated hazardous liquid pipeline rupture and release, Marshall, Michigan, 25 July 2010 (NTSB Pipeline Accident Report PAR-12/01)
organisations: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
outcomes: A 30-inch crude oil pipeline (Line 6B) ruptured in a wetland during the last stages of a planned shutdown and was not discovered for over 17 hours, during which two startups pumped additional oil equal to 81 percent of the total release of an estimated 843,444 gallons into Talmadge Creek and the Kalamazoo River. Cleanup costs exceeded 767 million dollars by the adoption date, about 320 people reported symptoms consistent with crude oil exposure and there were no fatalities. The NTSB attributes the rupture to corrosion fatigue cracks under disbonded polyethylene tape coating and to pervasive organisational failures including deficient integrity management, and makes recommendations to regulators, the operator and standards bodies.
